A computed tomography scan of the head and neck with intravenous contrast showed mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and prominence of the adenoids and palatine tonsils. Flexible laryngoscopy showed patent nasal sinuses and mucosal edema without abscess or necrosis. case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

You are a clinical fact validation system. Given a medical case, dialogue history, and the clinician's latest utterance, evaluate the factual accuracy of the clinician's claim using NLI-based reasoning.

Determine the relation between the clinician's claim and the medically established facts for the case.
Output valid JSON only matching the schema below. No explanation outside the JSON.

Output schema:
{
  "overall_relation": "supported" | "contradicted" | "insufficient" | "mixed" | "unknown",
  "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low",
  "reasoning": "<substantive clinical reasoning, 3-5 sentences>",
  "evidence_gaps": ["<gap1>", ...],
  "optional_claim_checks": ["<specific sub-claim>", ...]
}

For "reasoning": give the distilled MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE for this turn (3-5 sentences) — the key clinical
facts that decide this case, WHY the clinician's claim holds this relation, and specifically what the
clinician is getting right, getting wrong, or missing. This reasoning is handed to the dialogue policy as
its grounded environment knowledge, so make it clinically informative, not merely a verdict.
For "confidence": how certain you are in this relation given the available evidence.

Relation definitions:
- supported: The clinician's claim is consistent with established medical evidence for this case.
- contradicted: The clinician's claim conflicts with established medical evidence.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:

  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.

  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.
